design_detail: Systematic review and frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021295352; protocol published) of double-blind randomized trials lasting at least 1 week of oral ADHD medicines given alone (amphetamines, lisdexamfetamine as a separate node, atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate, modafinil, viloxazine) against each other or placebo. Primary outcomes: change in systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg) and pulse (beats per minute) at the time closest to 12 weeks; ECG measures secondary. 102 trials: 61 in children and adolescents (13,315 participants) and 41 in adults (9387); median duration 7 weeks. The searches extend those of Cortese et al. (2018) from April 2017 to January 2024. Version of record (the corrected version of 29 May 2025).
can_establish: Average short-term (median 7 weeks) changes in blood pressure and pulse with each ADHD medicine compared with placebo and with each other in double-blind trials, separately for children and adolescents and for adults, with a certainty rating for most estimates.
cannot_establish: Long-term effects on blood pressure or heart rate (4 trials at 24 weeks, none longer); risks of heart disease, stroke, arrhythmia or death (not outcomes); how many people have large rises (aggregate data only; outlier analyses only in the appendix); effects in people with heart disease or at doses above licensed ranges; trial-based comparisons between medicines in adults (all adult trials were placebo-controlled).

sample.recruitment: Searches of BIOSIS Previews, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, Embase, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, OpenGrey, Web of Science Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform including ClinicalTrials.gov, from inception to 18 January 2024, without language or publication-date restriction; FDA, EMA and manufacturers' websites and the references of reviews and guidelines searched; authors and manufacturers contacted (p. 357). The original searches to 7 April 2017 (9948 records, as described by Cortese et al., 2018) and the updated searches (4752 records) gave 81 and 21 trials (Figure 1, p. 357).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Double-blind randomized trials in children and adolescents (5 to 17 years) or adults with a primary DSM (III to 5-TR) or ICD diagnosis of ADHD or hyperkinetic disorder; oral monotherapy for at least 1 week against another medicine or placebo; FDA-approved medicines within the maximum doses recommended by the most used guidelines, unlicensed medicines at any dose (p. 357).
sample.demographics: Children and adolescents: mean age 11 (SD 3); of available data 73% male and 27% female, 2% Asian, 15% Black, 71% White. Adults: mean age 35 (SD 11); 57% male and 43% female, 6% Asian, 6% Black, 79% White (p. 360). All but four trials recruited exclusively or mainly in high-income countries (p. 360).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; all but two trials contributed short-term data (p. 360).
sample.selection_effects: Short trials (median 7 weeks, IQR 5 to 9); 85% industry funded; sexual, racial and ethnic minorities probably under-represented and results by sex rarely available (pp. 360, 364). Whether people with cardiovascular disease could take part in the trials is not reported in the article; the authors say people with a personal or family history of it might have larger increases (p. 364).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Oral; licensed medicines within maximum recommended doses, unlicensed ones at any dose (p. 357). Sensitivity analyses restricted licensed medicines to FDA-licensed doses (p. 359). Amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine were separate nodes, combined in a further sensitivity analysis.

comparison.controls: Placebo or another medicine within trials. Children and adolescents: some head-to-head trials and a connected network (for blood pressure, 1 trial of amphetamines against methylphenidate and 3 of lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate; for pulse, none of amphetamines against methylphenidate). Adults: only placebo-controlled trials, so every comparison between medicines is indirect (Figure 2, p. 358; pp. 360–361).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (randomized trials). Transitivity was examined by comparing study year, sample size, mean age, proportion of males, sponsorship and risk of bias across comparisons (appendix pp. 12–17, not read) (pp. 358–359).

outcomes.instruments: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg) and pulse (beats per minute), primary; ECG heart rate, PR interval, QRS complex and heart-rate-corrected QT interval (QTc), secondary; rates of outlier values for blood pressure and pulse as defined in each trial, post hoc (pp. 357–358).
outcomes.validity_norms: How the trials measured blood pressure and pulse is not described in the article. Risk of bias assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with CINeMA (high, moderate, low, very low) (p. 359).
outcomes.operationalization: Mean difference (QTc: standardized mean difference) against placebo or between medicines at the time closest to 12 weeks; endpoint values preferred over change from baseline when both were reported (p. 358).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (7 outcomes plus 3 post hoc outlier outcomes, two age groups, every pairwise comparison).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; the included trials were double-blind. Screening, full-text assessment and extraction were done by two independent researchers (p. 357).

analysis.effect_sizes: Against placebo (mean difference, 95% CI, CINeMA certainty), children and adolescents: methylphenidate systolic 1.81 (1.05 to 2.57, moderate), diastolic 2.42 (1.69 to 3.15, low), pulse 3.88 (2.87 to 4.89 in Figure 3, 4.8 in the text and Figure 5; moderate); amphetamines 0.87 (−0.3 to 2.03), 1.93 (0.74 to 3.11, high), 1.78 (−0.12 to 3.69); lisdexamfetamine 1.76 (0.68 to 2.83, moderate), 2.29 (1.25 to 3.34, low), 4.17 (2.74 to 5.61, very low). Adults: methylphenidate 1.66 (0.38 to 2.93), 1.6 (0.29 to 2.91), 4.37 (3.16 to 5.59); amphetamines 2.3 (0.66 to 3.94), 1.91 (0.17 to 3.65), 5.18 (3.47 to 6.89); lisdexamfetamine 1.62 (−0.81 to 4.06), 3.07 (0.69 to 5.45), 5.07 (2.76 to 7.37); all adult estimates very low certainty. Between medicines, direction as printed (column medicine against row medicine): systolic amphetamines against methylphenidate −0.94 (−2.33 to 0.44, high) in children and adolescents and 0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72) in adults; diastolic methylphenidate against amphetamines 0.49 (−0.88 to 1.87, high) and −0.31 (−2.49 to 1.87); pulse amphetamines against methylphenidate −2.1 (−4.25 to 0.06) and 0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90); systolic lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate −0.06 (−1.17 to 1.06, moderate) and −0.04 (−2.79 to 2.71); diastolic methylphenidate against lisdexamfetamine 0.13 (−0.98 to 1.24, moderate) and −1.47 (−4.19 to 1.25); pulse lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate 0.29 (−1.24 to 1.83, low) and 0.69 (−1.92 to 3.3). None of these differences between the stimulants is significant. Heterogeneity was low or low-to-moderate for most outcomes in children and adolescents and moderate or moderate-to-high for most in adults; incoherence could not be assessed in adults (no closed loops).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Sensitivity analyses: (1) licensed medicines at FDA maximum doses plus unlicensed medicines at any dose; (2) licensed medicines at FDA maximum doses only; (3) QTc by Fridericia or Bazett correction; (4) amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine as one node (p. 359). Their results are only in the appendix (pp. 354–355) and are described by direction in the text (p. 362).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021295352; protocol published (BMJ Open 2022, reference 15) (p. 357). Outlier rates are labelled post hoc outcomes (p. 358); any other deviation is not described in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: Medium-term results, outlier rates, ECG comparisons between medicines, sensitivity analyses, heterogeneity and incoherence statistics, risk-of-bias domains and funnel plots are only in the appendix, which was not read. The text's summary of pulse comparisons between medicines leaves out significant differences shown in Figure 5 (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not stated; the authors note that clonidine had only two trials with 189 children and adolescents (p. 364).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over a median of 7 weeks, methylphenidate, amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine raised average blood pressure by about 1 to 3 mm Hg and pulse by about 2 to 5 beats per minute compared with placebo (the effects of amphetamines on systolic pressure and pulse in children and adolescents were not significant). Methylphenidate, amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine did not differ significantly from each other in either age group. Certainty was mostly moderate to low in children and adolescents and very low in adults.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion describe the average effects as relatively small and warn that individuals may have larger changes (pp. 355, 363–364), which matches the data. Gaps: (1) the Results text says there were no statistically significant pulse differences between medications other than atomoxetine against methylphenidate and viloxazine (p. 362), but Figure 5 marks as significant amphetamines against atomoxetine (−3.8 beats per minute) and against lisdexamfetamine (−2.39) in children and adolescents (p. 361); (2) the abstract's list and ranges of medicines that raised blood pressure or pulse leave out bupropion, which raised adult systolic pressure (3.72) and pulse (2.95) (pp. 355, 359, 361); (3) the Discussion's statement that ADHD medicines have direct effects on cardiovascular safety (p. 363) refers to short-term average changes in blood pressure, pulse and ECG measures, not to cardiovascular events, which were not studied.

timeline.event: Cortese et al. network meta-analysis of efficacy and tolerability, by this review's account the only earlier network meta-analysis with a cardiovascular outcome (blood pressure only) (p. 357); its searches to April 2017 form part of this review's evidence
Protocol published (Lannes et al., BMJ Open; reference 15 of the review; not read)
This network meta-analysis (search to January 2024), with a linked Comment in the same issue (p. 319; not read)

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the first network meta-analysis of a range of cardiovascular measures with ADHD medicines (p. 356). It shares searches, data and authors with Cortese et al. (2018), so the two are not independent. For amphetamines against methylphenidate it shows no significant short-term difference in blood pressure or pulse; adult comparisons are indirect and of very low certainty, and trials say nothing beyond 24 weeks.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials or target-trial-emulation cohorts following people for years on an amphetamine or methylphenidate at licensed doses, reporting the distribution of changes (how many people cross clinical thresholds for raised blood pressure or heart rate) and cardiovascular events, including head-to-head comparisons in adults.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Populations, medicines, comparators, outcomes and timepoints specified (pp. 357–358).
PROSPERO CRD42021295352 and a published protocol (p. 357). Outlier outcomes are labelled post hoc, but the article does not say whether there were other deviations from the protocol or justify them.
Only double-blind randomized trials, chosen because observational studies do not allow causal inference about the drugs' effects (pp. 356–357).

12 databases and registries without language or date restriction, regulators' and manufacturers' websites, reference lists and contact with authors and manufacturers; search to January 2024, published April 2025 (pp. 355, 357).
Titles and abstracts screened and full texts assessed by two independent researchers (p. 357).
Extraction by two independent researchers, disagreements resolved with a senior member of the team (p. 357).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The list of excluded records with reasons is stated to be in the appendix (pp. 20–290) (pp. 357, 360); the appendix was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Aggregate description in the article (trials by medicine and age group, ages, sex, ethnicity, duration, countries, funding); study-level characteristics only in the appendix (pp. 330–338), not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 for every trial; 81 of 102 at low risk or some concerns, domain-level results in the appendix (pp. 359–360).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding of the trials was extracted and reported: 87 of 102 industry funded (p. 360).

Random-effects pairwise and network meta-analyses with a common heterogeneity parameter; incoherence assessed globally (design-by-treatment interaction) and locally (node splitting); transitivity examined (pp. 358–359).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the effect of risk of bias on the estimates (no restriction to trials at low risk); risk of bias enters only the CINeMA certainty ratings.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: CINeMA certainty is attached to the estimates and discussed, for example the weak evidence behind the ECG findings (pp. 359–363).
Heterogeneity and incoherence reported by outcome (p. 362); dose sensitivity analyses address one source; the authors state that aggregate data did not allow moderators to be identified (p. 364).

Contour-enhanced funnel plots for comparisons with more than ten trials did not indicate small-study effects (pp. 359, 362); unpublished data were sought from sponsors and regulators because most trials were industry sponsored (p. 364).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funders' role and the authors' interests are declared (pp. 359, 364).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is unmet (items 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15 met; item 2 partly met) and one non-critical item is not met (12), which by AMSTAR 2 gives high confidence in the review's conduct. That is not high certainty in its estimates: by the review's own CINeMA ratings most adult estimates are of very low certainty, and every adult comparison between medicines is indirect. Cite for: short-term average changes in blood pressure and pulse with methylphenidate, amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine against placebo and against each other, by age group, with their certainty. Do not cite for: long-term effects, cardiovascular events, the proportion of people with large rises, or effects in people with heart disease.

key_findings.finding: 102 double-blind randomized trials: 61 in children and adolescents (13,315 participants, mean age 11) and 41 in adults (9387, mean age 35); median duration 7 weeks (IQR 5 to 9); 87 (85%) industry funded; 81 (79%) at low risk of bias or some concerns; all but four from high-income countries.

Children and adolescents, compared with placebo: methylphenidate raised systolic blood pressure by 1.81 mm Hg (1.05 to 2.57, moderate certainty), diastolic by 2.42 (1.69 to 3.15, low) and pulse by 3.88 beats per minute (2.87 to 4.89, moderate); lisdexamfetamine by 1.76 (0.68 to 2.83), 2.29 (1.25 to 3.34) and 4.17 (2.74 to 5.61); amphetamines raised diastolic pressure by 1.93 (0.74 to 3.11, high), while their effects on systolic pressure (0.87, −0.3 to 2.03) and pulse (1.78, −0.12 to 3.69) were not significant.
key_findings.note: The upper limit of methylphenidate's pulse effect is 4.89 in Figure 3 but 4.8 in the text (p. 362) and Figure 5 (p. 361); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Adults, compared with placebo: methylphenidate systolic 1.66 mm Hg (0.38 to 2.93), diastolic 1.6 (0.29 to 2.91), pulse 4.37 beats per minute (3.16 to 5.59); amphetamines 2.3 (0.66 to 3.94), 1.91 (0.17 to 3.65), 5.18 (3.47 to 6.89); lisdexamfetamine 1.62 (−0.81 to 4.06, not significant), 3.07 (0.69 to 5.45), 5.07 (2.76 to 7.37); all of very low certainty.

Amphetamines against methylphenidate showed no significant difference: systolic pressure −0.94 mm Hg (−2.33 to 0.44, high certainty) in children and adolescents and 0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72) in adults (amphetamines minus methylphenidate); diastolic 0.49 (−0.88 to 1.87, high) and −0.31 (−2.49 to 1.87) (methylphenidate minus amphetamines, as printed); pulse −2.1 beats per minute (−4.25 to 0.06) and 0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90) (amphetamines minus methylphenidate).
key_findings.locator: Figure 4, Methylphenidate row under Amphetamines (systolic) and Amphetamines row under Methylphenidate (diastolic) (p. 360); Figure 5, Methylphenidate row under Amphetamines (pulse) (p. 361)
key_findings.note: Signs follow the figures' rule (the medicine defining the column against the medicine defining the row). No CINeMA symbol is printed for the adult cells or for the pulse cell in children and adolescents.

key_findings.finding: Lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate showed no significant difference: systolic −0.06 mm Hg (−1.17 to 1.06, moderate) in children and adolescents and −0.04 (−2.79 to 2.71) in adults; diastolic 0.13 (−0.98 to 1.24, moderate) and −1.47 (−4.19 to 1.25) (methylphenidate minus lisdexamfetamine, as printed); pulse 0.29 beats per minute (−1.24 to 1.83, low) and 0.69 (−1.92 to 3.3).
key_findings.locator: Figure 4, Methylphenidate row under Lisdexamfetamine (systolic) and Lisdexamfetamine row under Methylphenidate (diastolic) (p. 360); Figure 5, Methylphenidate row under Lisdexamfetamine (pulse) (p. 361)

key_findings.finding: The text reports no significant differences between medications in rises of systolic or diastolic pressure in either age group; for pulse, atomoxetine raised it more than methylphenidate (1.70, 0.48 to 2.92, low) and viloxazine (2.79, 0.83 to 4.76, moderate) in children and adolescents. Figure 5 also marks pulse with amphetamines as lower than with atomoxetine (−3.8, −5.91 to −1.68, high) and lower than with lisdexamfetamine (−2.39, −4.78 to −0.01, low) in children and adolescents.

In children and adolescents some trials compared medicines directly (for blood pressure, 1 trial of amphetamines against methylphenidate and 3 of lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate); in adults all trials were placebo-controlled, so the networks were star shaped, every comparison between medicines is indirect, and incoherence could not be assessed.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2, panels A and C (p. 358); Results, 4th paragraph (p. 360, continuing on p. 361); Results, 10th paragraph (p. 362)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: when licensed medicines were restricted to their licensed ranges, only amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine were consistently associated with higher blood pressure than placebo in adults; the increases with atomoxetine or methylphenidate in adults were no longer seen, which the authors suggest may indicate dose dependency. Grouping amphetamines with lisdexamfetamine did not change interpretations. The numbers are only in the appendix (pp 354–55, as printed).

Post hoc outlier analyses: compared with placebo, amphetamines had higher rates of outlier pulse values in children and adolescents; lisdexamfetamine of outlier diastolic pressure and pulse in children and adolescents; methylphenidate of outlier systolic and diastolic pressure in children and adolescents and of outlier pulse in both age groups. Outliers were defined by each trial, and the numbers are only in the appendix (pp. 356–363).
Only four trials gave medium-term (24-week) results, reported in the appendix, and no trial reported long-term results.

ECG measures against placebo: amphetamines raised ECG heart rate in adults (6.95, 1.98 to 11.92) and shortened the PR interval in children and adolescents (−2.8 ms, −5.09 to −0.51); methylphenidate raised ECG heart rate (3.21, 0.76 to 5.65) and shortened the QRS complex (−1.48, −2.9 to −0.07) in children and adolescents and lengthened it in adults (4.3, 0.92 to 7.68, from one study at unlicensed doses); lisdexamfetamine raised ECG heart rate (4.63, 1.35 to 7.92) and QRS (1.78, 0.01 to 3.55) in children and adolescents. No medicine changed QTc in children and adolescents; in adults atomoxetine raised it (SMD 0.27).
key_findings.locator: Figure 3 (p. 359); Results, 8th and 9th paragraphs (p. 362); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 363)

key_findings.finding: Contour-enhanced funnel plots did not indicate small-study effects. Heterogeneity was low or low-to-moderate for all outcomes but QTc and heart rate in children and adolescents, and moderate or moderate-to-high for all but PR interval and QRS in adults; in children and adolescents there was local incoherence for systolic and diastolic pressure (2 [17%] of 12 comparisons each), pulse (4 [40%] of 10) and QTc (3 [33%] of 9).

The authors conclude that average effects are generally small but individual patients may have larger changes, and that blood pressure and pulse should be monitored before and during treatment with any ADHD medicine, not stimulants only; they note that aggregate data could not show who is at higher risk.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Interpretation (p. 355); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 363); Discussion, 7th and 8th paragraphs (p. 364)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text states that, apart from atomoxetine against methylphenidate and viloxazine in children and adolescents, there were no statistically significant differences between medications in pulse increases (p. 362); Figure 5 prints in bold, the mark for an interval excluding no difference, amphetamines against atomoxetine (−3.8, −5.91 to −1.68) and amphetamines against lisdexamfetamine (−2.39, −4.78 to −0.01), as well as modafinil against atomoxetine, lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate, in children and adolescents (p. 361).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should follow Figure 5. Among the stimulants, it shows lisdexamfetamine raising pulse more than the other amphetamines in children and adolescents, with low certainty and an interval reaching almost zero.

reporting_issues.issue: The upper confidence limit of methylphenidate's pulse effect in children and adolescents is 4.89 in Figure 3 but 4.8 in the text and in Figure 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 4.89 would round to 4.9, so one of the two values is a misprint.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists amphetamines, atomoxetine, lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate and viloxazine as raising haemodynamic values and gives ranges among them, leaving out bupropion, which raised systolic pressure (3.72, 0.05 to 7.4) and pulse (2.95, 0.08 to 5.81) in adults according to the Results and Figure 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's adult ranges are not the full range of significant effects.

reporting_issues.issue: Several cells of Figures 4 and 5 carry no CINeMA certainty symbol, including every adult cell comparing amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine with methylphenidate, although the legends assign one of four certainty ratings.
reporting_issues.consequence: The certainty of these comparisons cannot be taken from the article.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record; the corrected version first published online on 29 May 2025), Lancet Psychiatry 12(5), pp. 355–365 (all pages, including contributors, declarations, acknowledgments and references; text extracted and every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Figure 2 network plots and the cells of Figures 4 and 5 used on this card checked at 400 dpi). The appendix and the linked Comment (p. 319) were not among the files and were not read; the correction notice was not among the files (per the round brief it corrects one author's name only).
